catalog_quote: [p. 133] stress is assigned to the last heavy syllable in a word. If there are no heavy syllables the stress falls on the first syllable of the word. The last syllable in nouns is extra-metrical. The extra-metricallity of the last syllable in nominals means that this syllable is not counted, i.e. it never receives stress. ... [p. 134, 4.6.2 STRESS ASSIGNMENT RULES] Stress assignment in the Fulfulde of Maasina is described with the parameters set out by metrical phonology (Goldsmith 1990: 169-216, Hayes 1986). parameters for the metrical structure in Fulfulde*: 1. last syllable is extra-metrical in nominals 2. left-headed feet 3. quantity sensitive feet 4. unbounded feet 5. right-headed word level structure. The rules deriving the metrical structure according to these parameters predict that the stress falls on the last heavy syllable (before the last syllable in nominals) or else on the first syllable. ... A left headed foot is a unit of syllables where the first is prominent, it receives (secondary) stress. If the foot is left headed and there is no heavy syllable in a word, then the first light syllable of this word is the head of the foot. ... A right headed word level structure implies that the last foot in a word receives the word stress. ... [p. 135] It should be noted that a heavy syllable is defined as a syllable containing two morae and a syllable that is light contains only one mora.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Quantity-sensitive: primary stress goes on the last heavy (CVV or CVC, bimoraic) syllable of the word; in nominals the final syllable (usually the class suffix) is extrametrical and never stressed, in verbs it counts; if the word has no (eligible) heavy syllable, stress falls on the first syllable. E.g. rawaandu 'dog' -> ra.WAAN.du, pamarol 'small' -> PA.ma.rol, dillintaako -> penult -taa-. Stress is realized by amplitude plus a pitch change whose direction depends on sentence intonation (pitch drop in declaratives), which Breedveld argues misled Arnott/Noye into positing initial stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Each heavy syllable heads a left-headed unbounded foot and 'receives (secondary) stress'; the word-level structure is right-headed so the last foot's head carries main stress (p. 134). No further detail on secondary stress realization.
new_statements.exceptions: Discusses Arnott's and Klingenheben's listed exceptions (numerals, adverbs ammaa/korii, interrogatives ndeye/moye/kiye, negative verb forms, usoko 'welcome', masin) and claims her rule predicts them; interrogatives with final stress in Arnott remain unexplained ('perhaps the rising intonation of a question'); monosyllabic atonic words treated separately (4.7.3); CVVC syllables marginal.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule (nominal vs verbal words differ in extrametricality); citation forms receive declarative intonation, so the stressed syllable of an isolated word shows a pitch drop after a higher initial syllable; phrasal focus gives the stressed syllable relatively high pitch (4.6.1, 4.7). Appendix 2 reports vowels measured slightly longer under stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Breedveld 1995 describes the Fulfulde of Maasina (Maasinankoore, central Mali), i.e. exactly maas1239. Her section 4.6.1 reviews and rejects the word-initial-stress descriptions of Arnott 1965 (Gombe, Nigeria) and Noye 1974 (Diamaré, Cameroon) and partially endorses Klingenheben 1963 (Adamawa) and McIntosh 1984 (Kaceccereere, Nigeria) — those concern other Fula varieties (adam1253, nige1253 etc.), but the rule in 4.6.2 is stated explicitly for 'the Fulfulde of Maasina'.

sources.note: Ch. 4.6 'Stress' (pp. 130-137): rejects Arnott/Noye word-initial stress (they equated high pitch with stress); stress = last heavy syllable of the word, final syllable extrametrical in nominals, else first syllable; realized by amplitude + pitch change (lowering in declaratives); metrical parameters listed p. 134; foot heads get (secondary) stress; Fulfulde is not a tone language (4.7).
